newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Unilever signs coop deal with Hungary Caola.
newsitem.headline: Unilever signs coop deal with Hungary Caola.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch group Unilever's Hungarian unit signed a cooperation agreement with Hungarian cosmetics and household chemicals company Caola Rt, Unilever and Caola officials said on Tuesday.
The agreement, which still needs a clearance from the Competition Office, widens Unilever's product portfolio and allows it to expand in Hungary while opening new markets to Caola.
"The benefits are very clear, most importantly, we broaden our product portfolio in the market," Fergus Balfour, Unilever Chairman for Hungary and South Central Europe, told a news conference.
"Having access to the manufacturing facilities in Hungary gives us a number of advantages," he said, adding that "we have a better cost structure than with imports."

Under the agreement Unilever acquires part of Caola's brands, takes over the domestic and foreign distribution of these products and will also be responsible for the marketing, they said in a joint statement.
Caola said it would benefit from the opening of new markets.

"We sought a partner who could in parallel provide us with long-term and reliable markets and professional assistance necessary to meet international requirements," Imre Nagy, Caola's General Director, said.
The partners declined to say how much Unilever paid for the brands, but Nagy said the whole amount will be reinvested into the company.

The cooperation allows Unilever to expand its presence in Hungary, where it has four factories manufacturing margarine, frozen products, ice cream and detergents and where it will have invested $170 million by the end of 1997.
"We're always looking at ways of expanding our investments and cooperation with partners in Hungary because this is the best way to integrate into the Hungarian market," Balfour said.

The agreement reflects the continuation of joint work between Unilever and Caola, including the joint development of a toothpaste and the joint acquisition of Helia-D cosmetics division of Israel's Teva -owned Biogal drugs firm.

The cooperation leaves Caola's Hungarian ownership intact but will make it one of Unilever's most important central- and east European manufacturing and research and development centres, the statement said.

Unilever Hungary expected 34 to 35 billion forints of sales for 1995, up 25 to 26 percent over 1995, Balfour said. He said the profit/loss account have not yet been prepared but the "trend is sharply improving from previous years".
